CALIFORNIA ART PRESERVATION ACT — MORAL RIGHTS FOR FINE ART INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. · Untitled No. 4

DECLARATION AND PURPOSE
This information sheet concerns a work described as A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015., titled Untitled No. 4, created by Jordan Lee (the "work"). Pat Morgan is identified here as the work's current owner or possessor, for reference only. This sheet summarizes provisions of California Civil Code § 987, the California Art Preservation Act, which addresses the intentional physical defacement, mutilation, alteration, or destruction of certain works of fine art by someone other than the artist who created them, and the artist's related right to claim or disclaim authorship of such a work.

This sheet is an informational record only. It states general provisions of California Civil Code § 987 as written; it does not determine whether A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. meets that section's own definition of "fine art," does not determine whether any act taken with respect to A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. would or would not violate the section, and does not itself assert, waive, reserve, or enforce any right under § 987 or any other law. It is not legal advice and is not a substitute for reading the statute directly.

THE CORE PROHIBITION AND THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF “FINE ART”
California Civil Code § 987, known as the California Art Preservation Act, restricts who may intentionally alter or destroy certain works of visual art once they exist outside the artist's own hands. Subdivision (c)(1) states: "No person, except an artist who owns and possesses a work of fine art which the artist has created, shall intentionally commit, or authorize the intentional commission of, any physical defacement, mutilation, alteration, or destruction of a work of fine art." A related but separate rule addresses professionals who work on the piece: under subdivision (c)(2), "In addition to the prohibitions contained in paragraph (1), no person who frames, conserves, or restores a work of fine art shall commit, or authorize the commission of, any physical defacement, mutilation, alteration, or destruction of a work of fine art by any act constituting gross negligence. For purposes of this section, the term “gross negligence” shall mean the exercise of so slight a degree of care as to justify the belief that there was an indifference to the particular work of fine art."

Both rules apply only to a work meeting the statute's own, narrow definition of the protected category. Subdivision (b)(2) defines it as follows: "“Fine art” means an original painting, sculpture, or drawing, or an original work of art in glass, of recognized quality, but shall not include work prepared under contract for commercial use by its purchaser." Whether A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. falls within that definition — including whether it is of "recognized quality" and was not created under a commercial-use, work-for-hire arrangement — is a determination the statute leaves to be made under its own terms; this sheet does not make that determination.

THE ARTIST'S RIGHT TO CLAIM OR DISCLAIM AUTHORSHIP
Separately from its protection against physical alteration or destruction, California Civil Code § 987 also gives the artist a form of attribution right over a work of fine art. Subdivision (d) states: "The artist shall retain at all times the right to claim authorship, or, for a just and valid reason, to disclaim authorship of his or her work of fine art." This right sits within the same statutory section as the alteration and destruction protection described elsewhere in this document, rather than in a separate statute, and it applies to the same category of "fine art" that the section defines.

REMEDIES THE STATUTE AUTHORIZES, AND THE TIME LIMIT TO SUE
California Civil Code § 987 identifies specific remedies available to enforce the rights it creates. Subdivision (e) states: "To effectuate the rights created by this section, the artist may commence an action to recover or obtain any of the following:" followed by five enumerated items — "Injunctive relief."; "Actual damages."; "Punitive damages. In the event that punitive damages are awarded, the court shall, in its discretion, select an organization or organizations engaged in charitable or educational activities involving the fine arts in California to receive any punitive damages."; "Reasonable attorneys’ and expert witness fees."; and "Any other relief which the court deems proper."

The statute also sets a deadline for bringing such an action. Subdivision (i) states: "No action may be maintained to enforce any liability under this section unless brought within three years of the act complained of or one year after discovery of the act, whichever is longer."

FINE ART THAT IS PART OF A BUILDING
California Civil Code § 987 addresses separately the situation where a work of fine art has become part of a building. Where the work cannot be removed without substantial harm to it, subdivision (h)(1) states: "If a work of fine art cannot be removed from a building without substantial physical defacement, mutilation, alteration, or destruction of the work, the rights and duties created under this section, unless expressly reserved by an instrument in writing signed by the owner of the building, containing a legal description of the property and properly recorded, shall be deemed waived. The instrument, if properly recorded, shall be binding on subsequent owners of the building."

Where the work can instead be removed without substantial harm, subdivision (h)(2) ties the section's continued protection to a notice procedure: if a building owner intends to remove such a work and, in the course of or after removal, cause or allow it to suffer physical defacement, mutilation, alteration, or destruction, the section's rights and duties apply "unless the owner has diligently attempted without success to notify the artist, or, if the artist is deceased, his or her heir, beneficiary, devisee, or personal representative, in writing of his or her intended action affecting the work of fine art, or unless he or she did provide notice and that person failed within 90 days either to remove the work or to pay for its removal. If the work is removed at the expense of the artist, his or her heir, beneficiary, devisee, or personal representative, title to the fine art shall pass to that person."

If the work is removed at the expense of the artist, his or her heir, beneficiary, devisee, or personal representative, title to the fine art shall pass to that person.

expectedJSON.body: California Civil Code § 987 also fixes how long its protections last and the general rule for giving them up. Subdivision (g)(1) states that the rights and duties the section creates "Shall, with respect to the artist, or if any artist is deceased, his or her heir, beneficiary, devisee, or personal representative, exist until the 50th anniversary of the death of the artist." As to waiver, subdivision (g)(3) states that, subject to one exception, the rights and duties "Except as provided in paragraph (1) of subdivision (h), may not be waived except by an instrument in writing expressly so providing which is signed by the artist." The referenced exception — subdivision (h)(1) — applies specifically to a work of fine art that has become part of a building and cannot be removed without substantial harm, and is addressed separately in this document.
